c.tagline: Champagne capital of the world, crowned by a Gothic masterpiece

taxi.fareNote: Official metered taxis wait at ranks near the station and cathedral; can also be booked by phone or app.

emergency.note: The EU-wide emergency number 112 also works nationwide and connects to English-speaking operators.

avoid.reason: No tourist-relevant no-go areas; outlying housing estates like Croix-Rouge have a rougher reputation but are far from the sights.
Watch bags against pickpockets around the cathedral, Place Drouet-d'Erlon nightlife and the train station.

hood_desc: The historic core around the great Gothic cathedral where 25 French kings were crowned, packed with medieval lanes, museums, and champagne cellars open for tours.
Reims' liveliest strip, a long pedestrian square lined with brasseries, bars, and cafés that fills up every evening, especially on weekends.
A quieter southern quarter anchored by the Romanesque-Gothic Basilique Saint-Rémi, a UNESCO-listed abbey church and the city's oldest building.
Home to the restored Art Deco covered market hall, plus surrounding streets with local shops, bakeries, and produce stalls.
A leafy, upscale residential area bordering the Parc de Champagne park, with grand champagne-house mansions and a slower pace.
lodging: Best Western Hôtel de la Paix

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink.

transit.hours: Citura network runs roughly 5am-midnight; trams every 6-8 minutes at peak
transit.pay: Single tickets, day passes, or contactless bank-card tap on trams and buses; tickets also sold via the Citura app
transit.note: Two tram lines (A and B) link the station to outlying districts; buses cover the rest of the city

train: High-speed TGV from Paris Gare de l'Est, ~45 min direct to Reims Centre; TGV Champagne-Ardenne station on the outskirts also links to CDG airport and southern France
bus: FlixBus and regional coaches connect to Paris, Charleville-Mézières, and other regional cities

tip.r: A service charge is included by law in restaurant bills; rounding up or leaving a few euros for good service is appreciated but not required.

food.name: Biscuit rose de Reims
food.desc: A dry, pale pink finger biscuit made to be dunked in champagne without falling apart - the city's edible emblem since the 1690s.

places.name: Maison Fossier boutique
places.note: France's oldest surviving biscuit house, founded 1756 and sole keeper of the pink biscuit recipe.

places.name: Les Halles du Boulingrin
places.note: Art deco covered market where local bakers and grocers sell Fossier tins and pink-biscuit desserts.

places.name: Champagne bars off Place Drouet d'Erlon
places.note: Most bars serve the biscuits alongside a glass, which is exactly how locals eat them.

food.name: Jambon de Reims
food.desc: Shredded cooked ham pressed into a parsleyed jelly terrine and sliced thick - a rustic charcuterie starter that nearly vanished and came back.

places.name: Les Halles du Boulingrin
places.note: Charcutiers in the 1929 market hall still make the terrine; the best place to buy a slice.

places.name: Brasserie Le Boulingrin
places.note: Reims brasserie institution running since 1925, with regional charcuterie on the menu.

places.name: Cafe du Palais
places.note: Family-run since 1930, stained-glass ceiling and a menu of Champagne comfort classics.

food.name: Chaource
food.desc: A soft, bloomy-rind cow's cheese from Champagne, chalky at the centre and lactic - traditionally cut into cubes and eaten with a glass of bubbles.

places.name: Les Halles du Boulingrin
places.note: Fromagers here carry Chaource, Langres and Brie de Meaux at different stages of ripeness.

places.name: Brasserie Le Boulingrin
places.note: Serves a regional cheese course; a good pairing with a glass of still Coteaux Champenois.

places.name: Cafe du Palais
places.note: Champagne-first cafe where cheese plates are designed around what is in the glass.

food.name: Potee champenoise
food.desc: A winter one-pot of cabbage, root vegetables, smoked sausage and salt pork simmered together - the farmhouse cooking behind the champagne houses.

places.name: Brasserie Le Boulingrin
places.note: Old-school brasserie cooking, unchanged decor and a menu that still runs to regional stews.

places.name: Cafe du Palais
places.note: Reliable for hearty Champenois plates in a wonderfully cluttered 1930s room.

places.name: Bistros around Place Drouet d'Erlon
places.note: The main restaurant square, where several kitchens run regional dishes as daily specials.

food.name: Plateau de fruits de mer
food.desc: Tiered platters of oysters, langoustines, whelks and crab - a Reims brasserie ritual, since champagne and shellfish are a local pairing.

places.name: Le Bocal
places.note: Tiny dining room behind a fishmonger; the freshest shellfish in Reims, so book ahead.

places.name: Brasserie Le Boulingrin
places.note: Classic brasserie shellfish counter, with a shucker working out front in season.

places.name: Les Halles du Boulingrin
places.note: Buy oysters by the dozen from the market fishmongers to open yourself.

food.name: Champagne
food.desc: The reason the city exists: tastings in chalk cellars quarried by the Romans, running from grower cuvees to grande marque vintages.

places.name: Maison Mumm
places.note: Central house with a straightforward cellar tour and tasting, walkable from the station.

places.name: Taittinger
places.note: Tours descend into former chalk quarries and abbey crypts beneath the vineyards.

places.name: Le Wine Bar by Le Vintage
places.note: Bar with a wide by-the-glass champagne list, useful for comparing growers without a tour.

food.name: Ratafia de Champagne
food.desc: Grape juice fortified with marc from the same harvest and aged in barrel - sweet, nutty and drunk as an aperitif or with foie gras.

places.name: Le Wine Bar by Le Vintage
places.note: Pours ratafia and marc alongside champagne, so you can taste the region's whole range.

places.name: Les Halles du Boulingrin
places.note: Market wine merchants stock small-grower ratafia that rarely leaves the region.

places.name: Grower cellars, Montagne de Reims
places.note: Village producers on the Montagne almost all make a house ratafia to finish a tasting.

landmarks: Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Reims (Reims Cathedral)
The UNESCO-listed Gothic masterpiece where French kings were crowned, its smiling angel and Chagall windows crown a facade of more than 2,300 carved figures.
Palais du Tau
The former archbishops' palace beside the cathedral displays coronation treasures, royal banquet halls and original statuary from the cathedral's weathered Gothic facade.
Basilique Saint-Remi
A vast UNESCO-listed Romanesque-Gothic basilica holding the relics of Saint Remi, the bishop who baptized Clovis and set France's royal story in motion.
Taittinger Champagne Cellars
Descend into chalk galleries dug by Gallo-Romans and medieval monks, where millions of Champagne bottles age in cool, candle-lit UNESCO-listed crayères.
Domaine Pommery
An eccentric Elizabethan-style Champagne estate whose 18 kilometres of chalk cellars pair grand carved reliefs with contemporary art installations and celebrated tastings.
Porte de Mars
A monumental third-century Roman triumphal arch, the widest in the ancient world, still standing proudly at the edge of Reims' old town.
Musée de la Reddition (Surrender Museum)
Preserved war room where Germany signed its unconditional surrender on 7 May 1945, its original operations maps still pinned exactly as Eisenhower's staff left them.
Place Royale
An elegant 18th-century royal square of arcaded Louis XVI facades centred on a statue of Louis XV, Reims' most harmonious classical set piece.
Halles du Boulingrin
A daringly vaulted 1929 concrete market hall, restored to Art Deco glory, that hums with produce stalls, oysters and locals on market mornings.
Chapelle Foujita
An intimate Romanesque-style chapel entirely frescoed by Japanese-French painter Léonard Foujita after his baptism in Reims, a moving blend of East and West.

train.note: No direct international trains from Reims, though the connection is quick - TGV services reach Paris Gare de l'Est in about 45 minutes, from where Eurostar leaves from the neighbouring Gare du Nord. Champagne-Ardenne TGV station outside the city is on the high-speed line toward Strasbourg and has direct services to Charles de Gaulle airport. SNCF advance fares open around six months ahead.

bus.note: Coaches stop near the station and at the Champagne-Ardenne TGV park-and-ride. FlixBus and BlaBlaCar Bus run to Paris, Brussels and beyond, though the TGV is much faster to Paris. Local buses and champagne-house shuttles serve Épernay and the vineyard villages.

ferry.note: Reims is inland in Champagne with no navigable passenger route - the Canal de l'Aisne à la Marne carries pleasure boats only, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Épernay
half.blurb: The Avenue de Champagne about 30 minutes away is lined with the cellars of major Champagne houses offering tours through chalk tunnels.

half.name: Laon
half.blurb: A hilltop cathedral town about 50 minutes north has a well-preserved medieval upper city ringed by ramparts, reached by a cable-guided funicular.

half.name: Verdun
half.blurb: A town about an hour and 20 minutes east sits amid the World War One battlefields, forts, and the Douaumont ossuary.

half.name: Troyes
half.blurb: A city about an hour and 45 minutes southwest has a well-preserved medieval center of half-timbered houses and Gothic churches.
